chunk_findings.detail:
`expect` is normalized by dropping an empty `mcp_servers` dict, but `after` is not, so any config that contains a bare `[mcp_servers]` header makes the safe cut look unsafe and the refresh is refused. Concrete input:

```
[mcp_servers]
[mcp_servers.foo]
command = "old"
```

The header regex never matches `[mcp_servers]` (no `.` after `mcp_servers`), so the loop keeps it and cuts only the `foo` block. `out` is `"[mcp_servers]\n"`; `tomllib.loads(out)` is `{"mcp_servers": {}}`, while `expect` was built as `{**before, "mcp_servers": {}}` and then had `mcp_servers` popped because the dict was empty, i.e. `expect == {}`. `after != expect`, so line 693 returns `None` and the caller refuses with "replace it by hand" — even though this is exactly the plain-table form the change is supposed to refresh, and the cut is semantically identical to `expect`. The bug B662a1ace82 therefore is not fixed for any config that declares the `[mcp_servers]` parent table. Normalizing both sides (e.g. also dropping `after["mcp_servers"]` when it is empty) is needed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions.py:690-693 (`_toml_without`, `expect`/`after` comparison)

chunk_findings.detail:
The skip region ends only at the next line whose `lstrip()` starts with `[`, so comments and blank lines between the removed table and the next header are absorbed into the cut, and the comment directly above the removed table is kept. With

```
# config for foo
[mcp_servers.foo]
command = "old"

# config for bar
[mcp_servers.bar]
command = "b"
```

the loop keeps `# config for foo`, skips the `foo` block *and* `# config for bar`, then keeps `[mcp_servers.bar]`. `out` is

```
# config for foo
[mcp_servers.bar]
command = "b"
```

The comment that documented the removed server is now attached to the following server, and that server's own comment has been deleted. `after == expect` still holds (comments don't affect parsing), so the corrupted output is accepted and written. The cut is supposed to remove the table, not relocate/delete neighbours' comments.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions.py:675-681 (`_toml_without`, skip-boundary loop)

chunk_findings.detail: The test's input is a config where `[mcp_servers.context7]` holds `command = "old-launcher"` — i.e. a stale launch under the companion's id, which is precisely the condition this change exists to fix. Because a second entry `[mcp_servers.ctx]` happens to carry the registry launch, the test asserts `status == "unchanged"` and `p.read_text("utf-8") == before`, so after `companions add` the file still contains `[mcp_servers.context7]\ncommand = "old-launcher"`. That is the un-fixed behavior the change's own docstring describes ("the TOML path answered 'already registers' over `.codex/config.toml` holding an old launch line and left it") and contradicts the stated intent ("refresh a stale TOML entry under the companion's id"). Anyone who asks for the `context7` server still gets `old-launcher` spawned. Not duplicating the launch under `ctx` is a legitimate goal, but the way to honour both goals is to cut (or rewrite) the stale `[mcp_servers.context7]` table and report that the launch already exists as `ctx`; asserting byte-for-byte equality of the config enshrines the residual bug instead. With input `<ctx entry present>` + `<stale context7 entry>`, the test pins `register` to leave the stale table in place.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_toml_without` refuses (returns `None`) for a safe cut whenever removing `cid` empties `mcp_servers` but an explicit `[mcp_servers]` parent header remains in the text. `expect` drops the now-empty `mcp_servers` key (`if not expect["mcp_servers"]: expect.pop("mcp_servers")`), but `after` still contains `{"mcp_servers": {}}` because the leftover `[mcp_servers]` header is not matched by `header` (the regex requires `mcp_servers\s*\.\s*<cid>`, so `[mcp_servers]` is kept) and therefore still contributes an empty dict to the parse. The two dicts are unequal, so the equality guard rejects an otherwise valid cut.

Reproduce with `.codex/config.toml`:
```
[mcp_servers]
[mcp_servers.foo]
command = "run"
```
and `cid="foo"`. The loop drops lines 2–3, `out` becomes `"[mcp_servers]\n"`, which parses to `{"mcp_servers": {}}`; `expect` is `{}` after the pop; `after != expect`, so `_toml_without` returns `None`, and the caller declines instead of cutting and appending the registry launch. This is wrong by the function's own docstring ("text minus every `[mcp_servers.<cid>]` table and sub-table"): the subtraction is well-defined and the result parses, so the refusal is spurious and the stale entry (B662a1ace82) stays in place for any config that has a hand-written `[mcp_servers]` parent header. The same mismatch occurs for `_toml_without("[mcp_servers]\n", cid)` with `cid` absent (empty `mcp_servers`), which likewise returns `None` although nothing needs cutting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions.py:678 (`_toml_without`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The TOML half of `register` invokes the pre-existing helper as
`_launched_elsewhere((tomllib.loads(text)["mcp_servers"], text), c, rel)`, wrapping the
mcp-servers mapping together with the raw file text into a two-element tuple as the
`data` argument. The helper is the one introduced for the JSON half of the same
refresh (`B-fix-companions-id-entry`), where the argument is the mcp-servers mapping
itself — "under another name" is expressed by iterating that mapping's names/entries.
Passing `(mapping, text)` instead means the helper either iterates the two distinct
objects (`data.items()` / `data[name]` on a tuple) or, if it tolerates the shape,
can never see an entry: given a config that already contains this companion's launch
under a second id `context7-clone` *and* a stale `[mcp_servers.context7]` table, the
guard intended to return `"unchanged"` (per the inline comment "unless the same launch
already runs under another name") does not fire, so `_toml_without` cuts the table and
the launch is appended again, defeating the second-copy protection. The first argument
must be just the parsed `mcp_servers` mapping, consistent with the JSON path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions.py:760 (`_launched_elsewhere` call in `_register_toml`)

chunk_findings.detail:
With `.codex/config.toml` containing both

```
[mcp_servers.context7]
command = "old-launcher"

[mcp_servers.ctx]
command = "<registry command>"
args = [...]
```

`CO.register(repo, context7, "codex")` returns `("unchanged", "… `ctx` …")` and the test asserts the file is byte-for-byte identical to `before`. That means the stale `[mcp_servers.context7]` table still launches `old-launcher` after the command that was supposed to fix exactly this: the commit's stated goal is "companions add refreshes a stale TOML entry under the companion's id … Cut the old table out and append the registry launch". Here the id under repair (`context7`) is left pointing at the old launcher, and the returned status `"unchanged"` positively asserts that nothing needed changing, so the user is not even told the entry is stale. The "launch already present under another id" short-circuit runs before the new stale-cut/append logic, so the refresh is skipped in precisely the case the bug B662a1ace82 describes (the TOML path answering "already registers" over an old launch line and leaving it). The test does not catch this; it codifies it as expected, so the fix is incomplete for any config that already contains the registry launch under a different server id.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_squash_on` treats "a commit on `ref` with the same patch-id as the item's landing commit" as proof that the item shipped on `ref`, but `git patch-id --stable` is a hash of the *change content only*: git documents that with `--stable` the output "does not depend on ... the line numbers within the files" (and, without `--verbatim`, on file names). It is therefore not a unique fingerprint of a logical fix — any two commits that add/remove the same lines collide.

Concrete failure: item `B20d45f540c` fixes bug B20 by adding

```
+    if x is None:
+        return None
```

which is squashed onto main as commit `M`. Later, an unrelated commit `U` on `develop` (in the same file, or any file — file names are not hashed) adds those exact same lines for different reasons. `_patch_ids(repo, "-n", "1", M)` yields `{pid: M}`, `_line_patch_ids(repo, tip)` yields `{pid: U, ...}`, and because `next(iter(mine))` is that `pid`, `_line_patch_ids(...).get(pid)` returns `U`. `_squash_on` returns `U`, so `reached()` reports B20 as shipped on `develop` (and on every release cut from `develop`) even though the hotfix was never back-merged. Version planning then claims the fix is present in releases that do not contain it. The only guard the author added is the exact-id subject match in the fallback path; the primary, content-based lookup has no such guard, so one-line/boilerplate fixes (identical guards, version bumps, `return None`, log lines) can silently cross-match. A stronger criterion would require corroboration (e.g., the `back-merge <id> into` subject, or a patch-id match whose subject/author references the item) rather than accepting patch-id equality alone.

chunk_findings.detail:
The second parametrized case is `('
[[macro]]
name = "x"
prompt = 
', "x")`, and the test body does `assert "unknown prompt" in msg and "not loaded" in msg and why in msg` with `why == "x"`. But `_get(repo, "x")` requests the prompt named `"x"`, so the error message always contains `unknown prompt 'x'` no matter what the appended `not loaded:` note says. The `why in msg` clause is therefore unconditionally true for this case and cannot fail. Given a syntactically broken config (a TOML parse error at `prompt = `), the assertion passes even if `macro_problems`/`not_loaded_note` emit a note whose text omits the actual parse-error reason entirely — i.e. the case does not exercise the property it claims to ("names why the macro config could not be loaded"). The only real guards in that case are that the message contains the literal strings `unknown prompt` and `not loaded`, so a regression that replaced the real cause with a generic non-empty note would not be caught. (The first case, `why == "unknown field"`, is not vacuous because that string is not part of the requested name.)
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_prompts_macro_error.py:37

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `why in msg` is vacuous for the parse-error case. The request name is `"x"` (`_get(repo, "x")`), and the MCP error is `f"unknown prompt {name!r}. Known: ..."` → `"unknown prompt 'x'. ..."`, so `"x" in msg` is true no matter what `macro_problems` reported for the parse error. Given that a TOML parse error cannot normally name the offending macro, this parameter was presumably meant to prove the child `[[macro]]` is identified, but it only matches the prompt name echoed by the error. A regression where the parse-error reason is wrong/generic (e.g. any `not loaded: ...` text) would still pass this case; only the presence of the literal `"not loaded"` is actually checked. Using a `why` string unique to the parse error (the decoder message, or the config file path) would make the case meaningful.
